newsitem.title: HAITI: Disillusioned Haitians stay away from polls. [CORRECTED 02:40 GMT 7/4]
newsitem.headline: Disillusioned Haitians stay away from polls. [CORRECTED 02:40 GMT 7/4]

text.p: In a silent protest against unrelenting hardship and poverty, Haitians on Sunday stayed away in huge numbers from Senate and local elections in the poorest country in the Americas.

The undeclared boycott of the fifth election in Haiti since a military regime was ousted in 1994 showed a deep disillusionment with the country's politics and frustration that life is getting even more difficult.

"I am a poor man. Why should I vote to put people who are already rich in power. First they have to give me a job. I cannot even buy a cup of rice to feed myself," said one man outside his hovel in the slum of Cite Soleil.
Added his friend: "Why vote for the 'Gran Manje'." -- Creole slang for corrupt politicians known as "Big Eaters".
A low turnout had been expected but foreign observers were surprised by how low it was. One said the most voters she had seen in a station at the same time was 11.

"You could say 'miminal' would be an accurate description," said Michael Magan of the U.S. International Republican Institute, which monitored the polls. Turnout appeared to higher in the countryside, he added.
Alexandre Lavaux, secretary general of the Provisional Electoral Council, did not have a total turnout figure but he said there had been no serious outbreaks of violence.
"It is not our responsibilty to comment on the success of the elections," he told a news conference.
More than 4 million (corrects from 254,843) people were registered, according to Council figures.

Reporters visiting polling stations in Cite Soleil in the afternoon were told that at one station 10 people had voted all day and at another only five out of 302 registered voters cast their ballot. Local radio reports from elsewhere in the country said more people had voted in some departments but not in great numbers.
President Rene Preval voted in mid-morning in the capital Port-au-Prince, saying: "This is an important moment. It expresses the will of the nation."

Much of the anger is focused on his plans to privatise state services, which are backed by international donors but could mean job losses in a country where 70 percent of the work force is unemployed and average yearly income is $250.
Social services are virtually non-existent and the infrastrucure is in ruins. Preval's pledge to turn Haiti into a "giant construction site" has not yet become a reality.

"(The people) voted for candidates and when they came into power, candidates voted for privatisation laws. We are in a situation where people don't believe anymore," said Lebrun Ruoat, chief electoral supervisor at a Port-au-Prince school where poll officials outnumbered voters.
At stake were nine seats in the 27-seat Senate, two parliamentary seats, 133 town delegations and 565 district assemblies.
Some people did want to vote. In Cite Soleil, shouting matches erupted at one polling station when about 20 people were prevented from casting their ballots.
An electoral officer said they were registered elsewhere. "These people are just here to cause trouble," he said.
But one of them, Alexi Fequanoit, said: "We want to vote. We want to vote against this economic coup d'etat."
He and his colleagues were supporters of Famni Lavalas, formed in November after a split in the ruling Lavalas Political Organisation.

It is led by former president Jean-Bertrand Aristide, a champion of the poor who was ousted by the military in 1991, and restored by a U.S.-led multinational intervention in 1994. He was succeeded by Preval after elections in December 1995.
Famni Lavalas opposes privatisation but the boycott suggested a degree of exasperation with that group too. Even in its stronghold Jacmel on the south coast turn-out was low, reporters said.
The Organisation of American States observer team said the elections were "calm and without serious incidents" and only scattered irregularities and problems occurred.
